A floating history tour of Lake George’s islands

A 22-year-old author brings his research to Lake George, navigating the islands full of history.
by Brianna KimmelAugust 21, 2026August 21, 2026

Share this:

  • Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook
  • Email a link to a friend (Opens in new window) Email
  • Share on Reddit (Opens in new window) Reddit
  • Share on X (Opens in new window) X
Listen to audio version of this article
0:00 / 4:17
Instaread

Cruising through the island-dense Narrows of Lake George, passengers aboard the Lake George Association’s Floating Classroom pass around historical photographs and laugh about legends of bygone rattlesnake infested hotels. Guiding the tour is Noah Chirnomas, a 22-year-old author bringing the research from his new 300-page book directly to the water.

Chirnomas spent three years researching and writing “The Islands of Lake George: Exploring the History and Mysteries.” His passion for the lake dates back to childhood memories of summers spent with his family on Lake George.

“I remember looking over a map when I was 8 years old, eagerly learning the name of every island,” Chirnomas said. “I wondered how they got those names.”

His first book, “Dome Island: Forever Wild on Lake George,” was published when Chirnomas was 18. Written while COVID-19 interrupted his high school education, Chirnomas used his spare time to uncover the history of his favorite Lake George island.

Searching for information

Chirnomas’ work on his new book took place while he attended Muhlenberg College in Allentown, Pennsylvania. There, he double majored in accounting and finance. Along with hundreds of hours spent combing through old family photo albums and newspaper clippings, Chirnomas traveled to Lake George as often as he could. For a few days at a time, he kayaked out to explore the islands on foot. 

“Looking back, sometimes I don’t know where I found all that time” Chirnomas said.  “But I think it’s just one of those things where when you love something, you find the time for it.”

Chirnomas became well acquainted with Lake George’s local libraries, museums and historical societies. He also took trips to the New York Public Library and the Philadelphia Art Museum. There, he scoured their special collections for information on some more illusive islands.

“Sometimes I think of this like putting a large puzzle together, with all these pieces scattered about many different places,” Chirnomas said. “So it provided a fun challenge to try to put those together and try to make as comprehensive a history of the islands as I could.”

An afternoon of learning

Leading the Lake George Association’s Floating Classroom this summer has given Chirnomas a chance to take passengers on an immersive tour of some of the lake’s hundreds of islands.

Passengers boarded a large pontoon boat at Rogers Memorial Park in Bolton Landing. They headed northeast towards the Narrows, a stretch of central Lake George where Chrinomas estimates nearly 50 islands are stationed. During the two hour boat ride, Chirnomas presented the names of landmark islands. He shared tales of their names and lore about their ownership and legends of their historical happenings.

For many of the islands Chrinomas discussed, he passed around photographs of bygone cottages and hotels that once stood on formerly privately owned islands. On each photograph was a description, handwritten in ink by Chrinomas. In addition, he shared printed images of maps, paintings and a steamboat ticket to 14 Mile Island from 1903.

Today, a majority of Lake George’s islands are owned by the state of New York. According to Chironmas, only about a dozen privately owned islands were sold prior to 1876. The first half of the tour focused on the state-owned islands, and their previous histories of private ownership. The latter half allowed passengers a closer look at few privately owned islands.

Those who attend

Ellen Wetherbee, who leads the Floating Classroom tour in the fall and spring, said it was a special treat to learn about the islands’ histories. Her program is primarily built to teach school-age children about the importance of water clarity on Lake George.

She shared additional anecdotal information as the tour progressed, prompting Chirnomas to mention Georgia O’Keeffe’s connection to Lake George via her then-husband, Alfred Stieglitz.

Chirnomas said many of the attendees of his tours have been natives or longtime locals of Lake George. He said he’s enjoyed the opportunity to reveal the islands’ hidden histories to passengers who are personally familiar with the lake.

“It’s also fun to continue learning from others and locals that I meet as well,” Chirnomas said. “This community has a shared commitment to wanting to protect the landscape and the water quality of the lake.”
